title: Under the fig tree (John 1:43–51)
hook: Nathanael asks can anything good come from Nazareth

segments.voice: Yesterday, Agnus Dei at the river, and two disciples who followed. Your line was what seek you. Did you ask yourself what you were really seeking? Day four hundred ninety-five.

Some towns come with a reputation. The one up the highway with nothing but a gas station. The neighborhood a family warns its kids about. The state that's the punchline of the joke. Then a friend runs up, breathless: we've found him, the one Moses and the prophets wrote about, and he's from there. That's today's scene. A man named Philip has just been called. He goes straight to his friend Nathanael with the news. And Nathanael, hearing the name of the hometown, says out loud exactly what he thinks of it.
screen: `A TOWN WITH A REPUTATION.` → `PHILIP: WE'VE FOUND HIM.` → `HE'S FROM NAZARETH.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims, Nathanael answers: "Can any thing of good come from Nazareth?" That's the whole of his review of the place. Philip doesn't argue. He uses the words Jesus said to the first two disciples the day before: come and see. And Nathanael comes. As he walks up, Jesus says of him: "Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no guile." No guile, no trickery. It's almost a joke: the man who just insulted Jesus's town is praised for being honest. He said exactly what he thought. Nathanael is startled. How do you know me? And Jesus says: before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you. We aren't told what happened under the fig tree. The text is silent. Some readers imagine Nathanael was praying or studying there. But nobody knows. What matters is that Nathanael knows, and it undoes him. In one breath the skeptic says: Rabbi, thou art the Son of God, thou art the King of Israel. And Jesus answers: you believe because I said I saw you under the fig tree? You will see greater things than these. An old tradition identifies Nathanael with the apostle Bartholomew. If that's right, the man who sneered at Nazareth became one of the twelve. The good thing came from the place he'd written off.
screen: `CAN ANY GOOD COME FROM NAZARETH?` · `NO GUILE: HE SAID WHAT HE THOUGHT.` · `I SAW YOU UNDER THE FIG TREE.` · `THE SKEPTIC BECOMES AN APOSTLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give a place you dismiss a chance. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a place you've written off. A town, a neighborhood, a school, a kind of church, a corner of the internet, even a person's whole background. Notice if a little sneer comes with it. Don't scold yourself. Just look at it. Now picture one good person from there, real or imagined, walking toward you the way Nathanael walked toward Jesus. If you pray, you can ask to see that place more truly. The bell holds the time.
Fig tree. Where Jesus said he saw Nathanael before Philip even called him. The Gospel never says what happened there. Today's word.
Your line: can any good thing come. Today, catch yourself once dismissing a place or a person, and answer your own question: come and see. Day four hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Bartholomew on August 24, and on that day the Mass reads this Gospel of Nathanael under the fig tree, following the old tradition that they are the same man.

fork.setup: you're Philip. you've told your friend you've found the one the prophets wrote about, and he scoffs at the man's hometown. what do you do?
options: drop it and go back alone.
fork.reveal: Philip just says come and see. Nathanael comes, is seen, and within a few lines calls Jesus the Son of God.

original.note: Greek: fig tree (John 1:48), where Jesus says he saw Nathanael.

trapdoor: what you thought: Nathanael was a cynic who got scolded.
what it means: Jesus praises his honesty, and the skeptic becomes one of the first to call him Son of God.
what a scholar hears: the fig tree scene is left unexplained, and Nathanael's link to Bartholomew is tradition, not text.

notes: The carry 'can any good thing come' echoes the KJV ('Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?'); the voice quotes the Douay. Kept as the index has it.
Douay verse numbering for John 1:45–47 may be offset by one from the KJV; confirm the refs.
Rabbis studying under fig trees: later rabbinic material (e.g., Midrash); stated as 'some rabbis in later centuries'. Confirm or cut.
Nathanael = Bartholomew: a tradition from the 9th century onward and used in the Roman Lectionary on August 24. Confirm the phrasing.
Nazareth not named in the Hebrew Bible: confirm.

Editor review (483-500 pass): Philip did not hear Jesus say 'come and see' (Jesus said it to the first two disciples, 1:39), so the line now says so; hook no longer says 'everybody' or 'imagine' or tells the listener what they've said; cut 'not named once in the Hebrew scriptures', 'nobody expected anything', the later-rabbis fig-tree claim, and 'Jesus smiles'; 'for many centuries' softened to an old tradition.
